analysis.one_liner: Exempts all paid work done in an employee's home from federal workplace safety law.
analysis.headline: The bill to exempt home workplaces from federal safety rules never got a committee vote and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 so that none of its rules — inspections, safety standards, recordkeeping — apply to any work performed in a worker's own residence. That would cover not only office telecommuting but any paid work done at home. It was introduced by Rep. Clay Shaw of Florida with 42 Republican cosponsors in January 2000, sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who have people working from home would gain the most: they would no longer face any federal occupational safety duties for home workplaces, ending the possibility of OSHA standards, inspections, or recordkeeping requirements there.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new clause to the Occupational Safety and Health Act saying 'Nothing in this Act shall apply to employment performed in a workplace which is located in the residence of the employee.' [S3]
The CRS summary describes the same change: making the Act inapplicable to employment performed in a workplace located in the employee's residence. [S2]

For employers, this would settle the question raised by a late-1999 OSHA advisory letter about employer responsibilities for home offices — by removing OSHA's jurisdiction entirely rather than by clarifying what it covered. The letter had already been withdrawn in January 2000 after heavy criticism.

analysis.who_pays: Home-based employees would lose coverage under federal workplace safety law for all work done in their residence — the standards, inspections, and recordkeeping that protect people at work would simply stop applying to them. That matters least for a home computer and most for low-wage industrial homework like assembly or sewing done at home.

drawbacks.text: The exemption is written broadly: it covers 'employment performed in a workplace which is located in the residence of the employee,' not just clerical telework, so it strips safety-law coverage from all paid home work, including industrial homework. [S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge that OSHA's advisory letter that prompted the bill had already been withdrawn in January 2000, removing the immediate concern the bill was aimed at; the legislation would have permanently barred OSHA from the home workplace instead of resolving a specific dispute.
Because home workplaces would be entirely outside the Act, workers injured doing paid work at home could no longer rely on OSHA's hazard standards as a backstop for those conditions. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For businesses, the bill offered certainty: no federal safety obligations for home-based staff. The cost falls on home-based workers, who would give up federal safety coverage for any work done in their residence. The public benefit is thin because OSHA rarely inspected home offices even before the bill, and the advisory letter that sparked the controversy had already been pulled; the lasting effect would be a permanent carve-out from the nation's workplace safety law.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, and neither the subcommittee nor the full committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Clay Shaw (R-FL) introduced the Home Workplace Preservation Act on January 24, 2000, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S5]
On February 14, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections. [S5]
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a subcommittee or committee vote, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001. [S5]

The immediate dispute behind the bill — a 1999 OSHA advisory letter discussing employer responsibilities for home-based work — had already been resolved when OSHA withdrew the letter in January 2000 after public criticism.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers got what they most wanted anyway: the OSHA advisory letter was withdrawn, and the statutory exemption never needed to pass. Because the bill died, home-based workers kept their formal coverage under federal safety law, though the episode made clear how limited that coverage is in practice.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, whose target letter was already withdrawn

for.name: 42 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making all 43 supporters Republicans. [S4]

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Workforce Protections subcommittee and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Every listed supporter — the sponsor and all 42 cosponsors — was a House Republican, and the bill never reached a vote where Democrats could weigh in. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would remove every federal occupational safety obligation for work performed in an employee's residence, ending inspections, standards, and recordkeeping there. The gain comes directly from what home-based workers would lose: coverage under the federal safety law.
